newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai deposit run slows, measures seen working.
newsitem.headline: Thai deposit run slows, measures seen working.

text.p: A recent run on deposits at 10 troubled Thai finance firms has slowed down, and the market has calmed as investors digest new government measures, a central bank official said on Friday.

International Monetary Fund (IMF) managing director Michel Camdessus also lent his support to the Thai government, saying he was confident about the way the Thai authorities were handling the country's financial sector problems.

The total amount of money withdrawn from the 10 finance firms, which were told this week by the central bank to raise capital, slowed to 3.5 billion baht ($135 million) on Thursday, the official said.

This compared to withdrawals of about 6.0 billion on Wednesday and 4.4 billion on Tuesday. A central bank official estimated investors took out about 15 billion baht on Tuesday and Wednesday from these firms and other finance companies.
"The market seems to have calmed down and investors might come to realise that the measures imposed by the Bank of Thailand will eventually strengthen the sector," the official said.
The stock market rose slightly early on Friday, after plunging this week near to a 4-1/2-year low. It was up 3.36 points to 680.01 after the first 30 minutes of trade.
The Thai baht firmed early, trading around 25.948/25.950 to the dollar compared to 25.960/25.970 late on Thursday.
On Monday, Thai authorities shook up the finance sector by ordering 10 finance firms, hard-hit by a liquidity crunch, to raise capital by a total of 8.25 billion baht ($317 million).
They also told banks and finance companies to raise provisions for sub-standard loans, primarily to the depressed property sector, to 115 percent and 120 percent respectively from 100 percent.
"What they are doing is exactly what you must do to avoid the recurrence of a Mexico-like crisis," Camdessus told a conference in Hong Kong on Friday.
"The Thai authorities are taking gradual steps to address the kind of tensions which is only the other face of a very successful development policy," he said.

"I see them taking steps to address one of the vulnerabilities of the Thai economy...I am confident that the measures and the programme for the future will have the potential to carry the economy back on track for sustainable growth," he said.

A Thai newspaper reported on Friday that the government was set to issue zero coupon bonds in an effort to revitalise the sagging stock market, which has suffered following the finance sector shake-up.
The Bangkok Post gave few details, saying only that finance ministry officials said the zero coupon bonds would be sold to foreign investors.
Ministry officials were not immediately available to comment on the report.
